extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, and patent examiners (U.S. subject-matter-eligibility analysis)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether claimed inventions are directed to judicial exceptions (especially abstract ideas, mental processes, and mathematical concepts) under U.S. patent eligibility jurisprudence (Alice/Mayo framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to organizing human activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to schemes for organizing human activity or business practices (e.g., generating menus, taking restaurant orders, structuring a sales force, using advertising as currency, algorithms for scheduling visits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit treats such concepts as abstract ideas; merely implementing them using conventional computer components or describing them as performed on a device does not remove them from being abstract. Examples/case law: claims characterized as 'generating menus … or taking orders from restaurant customers' (Enfish/related discussion and 842 F.3d citations), In re Ferguson (structuring a sales force), Ultramercial v. Hulu (advertising as exchange), In re Maucorps (algorithm for number of visits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to managing human behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that embody methods for monitoring, guiding, or managing people’s actions (e.g., storing user pre-set spending limits and notifying users when limits are reached; filtering content; mental diagnostic procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have characterized tracking financial transactions, filtering content, or prescribed mental procedures for diagnosis as abstract ideas because they are methods of organizing human activity or mental processes. Examples/case law: Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (budgeting/tracking spending limits), BASCOM Global Internet v. AT&T (content filtering found abstract under step 2A), In re Meyer (neurologist's mental process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to tracking or organizing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that collect, classify, store, index, customize, encode/decode, analyze, or otherwise organize information (including tailoring content based on user data or time of day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting and organizing information is often treated as an abstract idea; tailoring content is analogized to traditional non-technical practices (e.g., newspaper inserts, TV scheduling). Examples/case law: BASCOM (content filtering), Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (webpage customization), TLI Communications (classifying/storing images), Electric Power Group v. Alstom (collect/analyze/display), RecogniCorp v. Nintendo (encoding/decoding image data), Digitech (mathematical correlations to organize information), Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec (email screening/distribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: An idea 'of itself' (uninstantiated concept / mental process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas include uninstantiated concepts, plans, schemes, and mental processes — things that can be performed in the human mind or with pen and paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts use the phrase 'an idea of itself' to describe standalone concepts or mental steps that are not tied to a particular concrete implementation; methods that can be performed mentally are unpatentable abstract ideas. Information and analysis steps are intangible and fall into this realm. Examples/case law: CyberSource Corp. v. Retail Decisions (mental processes), Gottschalk v. Benson, Mayo, Parker v. Flook, and many Federal Circuit decisions noting that collecting/analyzing/presenting information is abstract when not tied to a particular tool or improvement (e.g., Electric Power Group, Content Extraction & Transmission).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to data comparisons performable mentally
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims whose essential operation is obtaining and comparing intangible data in ways that humans could perform mentally or with pencil-and-paper (e.g., comparing genetic sequences, mapping transaction histories, grading/ comparing loan packages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim does not require particular computer implementation, courts may conclude the steps read on human mental activity and deem the claim directed to an abstract mental process. Examples/case law: CyberSource (credit-card transaction validation via comparing transaction data), Univ. of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics (comparing BRCA sequences), Mortgage Grader v. First Choice Loan Servs. (anonymous loan shopping). Other examples: collecting and comparing known information (Classen), diagnosing via clinical tests and analysis (In re Grams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to organizing/analyzing information analogous to mental work
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that organize or analyze information by steps analogous to human thought processes (e.g., translating functional descriptions, extracting and recognizing data from documents, detecting misuse via rule-based analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that can be performed mentally or are analogous to human reasoning are abstract unless they add significantly more (a technical improvement). Examples/case law: Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics (converting descriptions for logic circuits read on mental steps), Content Extraction (scanner + recognition + storage was viewed as data collection/recognition humans have long done), FairWarning (collect/analyze/notify to detect misuse). Additional examples: Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One Fin. (collect/display/manipulate data), Erie Indem. Co. indexing example, Versata pricing determination, RecogniCorp encoding/decoding, Digitech organizing via mathematical correlations, Return Mail, Internet Patents retention in navigation of forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts having no particular concrete or tangible form
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to ideas that are conceptual frameworks or building blocks without a concrete instantiation (e.g., using advertising as currency, organizational/product group hierarchies to determine price, assigning hair designs to head-shape zones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts characterize such claims as abstract because they are basic conceptual frameworks that lack a particular concrete application; these building-block ideas are patent-ineligible absent additional inventive concept. Examples/case law: Ultramercial (advertising as exchange), Versata (pricing via organizational/product hierarchies), In re Brown (haircutting method described as abstract).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships/formulas as judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts — algorithms, formulas, calculations, mathematical relationships — are treated as abstract ideas (a judicial exception) and have historically been characterized similarly to laws of nature or natural principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent treat mathematical formulas as non-statutory subject matter unless applied in a patent-eligible manner (e.g., Diehr noted that the Arrhenius equation itself is an exception). Examples/case law: Gottschalk v. Benson (binary-coded decimal conversion algorithm), Parker v. Flook (alarm-limit formula), Bilski (mathematical hedging formula), Alice (characterizing Flook as mathematical formula exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to a mathematical relationship or formula (specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite or depend on a specific mathematical relationship or formula (e.g., Arrhenius equation used to compute cure time) are directed to a mathematical concept and thus to an abstract idea/judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mathematical formula as claimed subject matter is an exception absent inventive concept in application. Example/case law: Diamond v. Diehr (Arrhenius equation in rubber-molding press: the equation itself is non-statutory), plus Benson, Flook, Mackay Radio & Tel. Co., Bilski.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to performing mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims whose core steps are mathematical computations or manipulation of data using formulae or calculations (e.g., computing policy values, manipulating data via formulas to create new forms) are treated as abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts view claims that amount to mere mathematical computation or manipulation of data as abstract ideas unless they effect a technical improvement. Examples/case law: Bancorp Services v. Sun Life (calculations for managing insurance policy values), Digitech (generating data by manipulating existing information using mathematical formulas), and other algorithmic examples (In re Maucorps, In re Grams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely presenting results of abstract processes is abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that only present the results of collecting or analyzing information, without identifying particular tools or improvements in how presentation is achieved, are considered part of the abstract-idea exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting results (e.g., display of analyzed data) without more does not render an otherwise abstract collection/analysis patent-eligible; courts look for a particular tool or an improvement in the functioning of the computer or technology. Examples/case law: Content Extraction & Transmission, Electric Power Group, Ultramercial citations noting presentation-as-ancillary and abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding conventional computer components or automation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply reciting generic computer components or automating a well-known human/business practice on a generic computer does not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has repeatedly held that claims that add conventional computer implementation to an abstract idea remain directed to the abstract idea absent an inventive concept that provides a technological improvement. Example language: claims described as 'adding conventional computer components to well-known business practices' remain abstract (cases cited throughout the discussion, e.g., restaurant-order device example, Alice, and related Federal Circuit decisions).
